title_options: Why Water Dances On A Very Hot Pan 💧

share.myth: The hotter the pan, the faster a water drop boils away.
share.truth: Above roughly 180 C, the drop's underside turns to vapour so fast that it floats on a film about 50 micrometres thick; the vapour insulates it, so it skates and lasts longer (Leidenfrost effect; Quéré 2013; Biance, Clanet & Quéré 2003).
share.line: On a hot enough pan, water doesn't touch the metal. It floats on its own steam, so it lasts longer.

facts: Quéré D 2013, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 45:197-215 (Leidenfrost dynamics): drops levitate on their own vapour, injected beneath the drop and pushed by its weight; with no solid contact they are highly mobile.
Lagubeau, Le Merrer, Clanet, Quéré (APS DFD 2008 lay paper): for water this happens above about 180 C; vapour film thickness about 50 micrometres.

Because vapour conducts heat poorly, a levitating drop evaporates far more slowly than one boiling in contact with a cooler pan (Biance, Clanet & Quéré 2003, Physics of Fluids 15:1632). The exact onset depends on the surface.
description: Flick water on a pan that's hot enough and it doesn't sizzle away. It skates around on a cushion of its own steam. #shorts #science #physics #kitchen
sources: Quéré 2013, Annual Review of Fluid Mechanics 45:197 (Leidenfrost dynamics); Biance, Clanet & Quéré 2003, Physics of Fluids 15:1632; Lagubeau et al., APS Division of Fluid Dynamics 2008.

scenes.narration: Flick water on a warm pan and it sizzles away. Make the pan much hotter, and the drops start to dance.
You'd think a hotter pan would boil them away faster. It doesn't.
Above about a hundred eighty degrees Celsius, the bottom of the drop turns to steam instantly.
That steam lifts the drop off the metal, on a layer about as thin as a human hair.
With nothing touching, the drop skates around almost without friction.
And steam is bad at carrying heat, so the floating drop boils away much more slowly.
It's called the Leidenfrost effect, and scientists still study how these drops move.
On a hot enough pan, water doesn't touch the metal. It floats on its own steam, so it lasts longer.
So why does a cooler pan make the water vanish faster?
